say.text: A 32-year-old man has had right lower abdominal pain for 14 hours. CT shows uncomplicated appendicitis, with no appendicolith.
He is fit and understands that some patients need surgery later. He asks what his options are. Which statement is right?

choices.label: Appendicectomy is the only treatment, so surgery is unavoidable
Antibiotics-first is an accepted option for him
Antibiotics-first suits every patient with appendicitis
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check each option against the stem: CT-proven, uncomplicated, no appendicolith, and a patient who accepts the trade-off. Which option fits that patient?
Yes. Current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis.
Appendicectomy is still the treatment of choice, so this is an option for selected patients, not a replacement.
Tempting: appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, and older exam keys wrote 'the only treatment', so the two blur together.
Not quite: current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease.
Which of the two statements is the old key, and which is current teaching?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two: treatment of choice is not the only treatment. This patient can be a candidate for antibiotics-first.

say.text: The old key says appendicectomy is the only treatment. Current sources give it as the treatment of choice, and accept antibiotics-first for selected patients.
Tempting: antibiotics-first is a real option, so the headline sounds right and the conditions drop out of memory.
Not quite: it is offered to selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease and no appendicolith. 'Every patient' drops those conditions.
Which condition in the stem does 'every patient' ignore?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifiers: selected patients, CT-proven, uncomplicated, no appendicolith. Drop one and the advice changes.

say.text: Antibiotics-first is accepted for selected adults. A significant proportion later need appendicectomy for recurrence, and an appendicolith predicts failure.
Now the why. You can offer this patient antibiotics first. Which reason fits?

choices.label: Only surgery removes the organ, so antibiotics can merely delay it
Antibiotics work the same whatever the scan shows, so it adds nothing
Inflamed but not perforated, with no appendicolith to block the lumen
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what makes a case uncomplicated, and what an appendicolith does to the inflamed appendix. Which reason uses both?
Yes. Uncomplicated means inflamed without gangrene or perforation. With no appendicolith, antibiotics have the best chance of settling the inflammation.
Tempting: surgery does remove the diseased organ, so it feels like the only real cure.
Not quite: appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, but antibiotics-first is accepted for selected uncomplicated cases.
What is it about this patient's appendix that makes non-operative care reasonable?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep both: surgery is the usual treatment, and it is not the only route for every case.

say.text: Antibiotics-first is for uncomplicated disease without an appendicolith. Those patients fail more often on antibiotics alone, and they are operated on.
Tempting: antibiotics do settle many inflamed appendices, so the scan looks like extra detail.
Not quite: the scan decides who is a candidate, through uncomplicated disease and no appendicolith. An appendicolith predicts failure.
Which feature of the scan would change your advice?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so give the scan its job: it shows whether the disease is uncomplicated and whether a stone is present.

say.text: The scan shows whether the disease is uncomplicated and whether there is an appendicolith. Without those two answers, antibiotics-first is not safe advice.
A 34-year-old man has CT-proven appendicitis with an appendicolith. He asks whether antibiotics alone could settle it.
What do you advise?

choices.label: Antibiotics alone, because the CT shows no perforation
Appendicectomy, because an appendicolith predicts antibiotic failure
Ochsner-Sherren regimen, because a mass may form
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The stem names one finding that predicts how antibiotics fare. Which option deals with that finding?
Yes. An appendicolith predicts failure of antibiotics and a higher risk of perforation, so this patient needs appendicectomy.
Laparoscopic appendicectomy is preferred where it is available.
Tempting: a scan without perforation looks reassuring, and antibiotics-first is a real option.
Not quite: an appendicolith predicts failure of antibiotics, so antibiotics-first is not offered here.
Which finding in the stem rules antibiotics-first out?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold the qualifier: CT-proven uncomplicated disease with no appendicolith. An appendicolith breaks that.

say.text: Antibiotics-first is for selected adults. Those with an appendicolith fail more often, and the stone predicts a higher risk of perforation.
Tempting: a regimen sounds gentle, and it avoids an operation for a patient who might be a candidate for conservative care.
Not quite: the Ochsner-Sherren regimen is for a formed appendicular mass, not for an inflamed appendix with a stone.
What does the stem describe: a mass, or an inflamed appendix with a stone in it?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two: the regimen is for a mass walled off by omentum. This patient has a stone in an inflamed appendix.

say.text: A mass is inflamed appendix walled off by omentum and bowel, and the regimen is for that. An appendicolith with an inflamed appendix needs appendicectomy.
A 45-year-old man has had right lower abdominal pain for five days. He has a tender, palpable mass in the right iliac fossa and a low-grade fever. He is stable.
What is your first step?

choices.label: Emergency appendicectomy tonight, before the mass settles
Laparotomy now, with open drainage of the mass
Ochsner-Sherren regimen with fluids and antibiotics
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether this is pus that needs draining, or a walled-off mass in a stable patient. What does the stem describe?
Yes. A stable mass is managed by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen: nil by mouth, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesia, and charting of the pulse, temperature and mass.
Surgery follows only if the pulse rises, pain or mass size increases, or peritonitis develops.
Tempting: a tender lump with fever looks like appendicitis that must come out now.
Not quite: a mass is stable and walled off. The regimen comes first, and surgery waits unless the patient worsens.
What would make you operate on this man, and has any of it happened?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold the order: stable mass first, operation only on deterioration.

say.text: Tempting: pus may be inside, so opening the abdomen to drain it sounds thorough.
Not quite: a mass is inflamed appendix walled off by omentum, with no drainable pus yet. Open drainage is a fallback for an abscess.
Is there pus to drain here, or a mass that needs time?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the mass from the abscess: a mass settles on the regimen, and an abscess is drained.

say.text: A mass is walled off by omentum and bowel. The regimen lets it settle, and surgery waits for failure. An abscess, which is pus, is drained, usually by image-guided percutaneous drainage.
An exam stem asks what to do about interval surgery once an appendicular mass has settled on conservative care.
Which answer fits both the exam key and current practice?

choices.label: Routine interval appendicectomy at 6–8 weeks for everyone
Traditionally 6–8 weeks, now selective; scan if older
No interval surgery or work-up is needed once it resolves
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The key has two halves: what the exam taught, and what is done now. Check each option against both halves.
Yes. PYQs expected interval appendicectomy at 6–8 weeks. Current practice makes it selective.
Colonoscopy or CT is advised in older patients, to exclude caecal carcinoma.
Tempting: 6–8 weeks is the timing you were taught, so routine surgery feels complete.
Not quite: the timing is the old key. Current practice is selective, and older patients need a work-up first.
What changes for an older patient before any operation?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold the old key with its update: routine 6–8 week surgery was taught, and it is now selective.

say.text: Tempting: the mass has resolved, so the problem seems over and no further step looks needed.
Not quite: a resolved mass in an older patient can hide a caecal tumour, so a check is needed before deciding.
Which patients need that check before you decide on surgery?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the check: older patients need colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma.

say.text: Older patients, over about 40, can have caecal carcinoma. Colonoscopy or CT excludes it first, and interval surgery is then chosen selectively.
A 55-year-old man's appendicular mass has resolved on the regimen. He is well and has no fever.
What is the next step?

choices.label: Routine interval appendicectomy at 6–8 weeks, no other work-up
Immediate appendicectomy, because the mass was a problem
Colonoscopy or CT for caecal carcinoma, then selective surgery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the age in the stem. What does that age add before you decide about surgery?
Yes. Over about 40, caecal carcinoma must be excluded before selective interval surgery. Age is the qualifier that changes the work-up.
Tempting: interval surgery is the scheduled step you were taught, so the date does the work.
Not quite: at 55 the work-up comes first. Colonoscopy or CT excludes caecal carcinoma, and surgery is then selective.
Which step does the age in the stem add?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so add the qualifier: over about 40 means work-up before the knife.

say.text: Tempting: a mass once meant trouble, so removing the appendix now seems safest.
Not quite: a mass that settles on the regimen is not an emergency. Surgery follows deterioration, or selective interval surgery later.
Is anything urgent happening in this man, and what does the stem tell you?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold the sequence: settle the mass, then decide on surgery with the work-up.

say.text: A mass that settles is not an emergency. Routine surgery at 6–8 weeks is no longer applied to everyone. Over about 40, colonoscopy or CT comes first.
A 40-year-old man has swinging fever and a tender right iliac fossa collection that can be drained on imaging.
What is the best treatment?

choices.label: Laparotomy and open drainage, with antibiotics
Ochsner-Sherren regimen alone, as for a mass
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether the collection is pus that a guided needle or tube can empty. What does the stem say about the route?
Yes. An abscess is drained under image guidance, usually percutaneously, with antibiotics.
Open drainage is kept for failure, or where imaging is not available.
Tempting: pus means open drainage, since the abscess is the thing to empty.
Not quite: open drainage is the fallback. The first choice is image-guided percutaneous drainage.
What route does the imaging in the stem point to?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold the order: percutaneous first, open drainage if that fails.

say.text: Tempting: the regimen treated the mass, so it seems to work for any collection in the iliac fossa.
Not quite: the regimen is stopped when a drainable collection forms, and that collection is then drained.
What does the stem add that changes the plan from a mass?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two: the regimen is for a mass, and a drainable abscess is drained.

say.text: A mass is walled-off inflamed appendix, managed by the regimen. A drainable abscess is pus, usually drained by image-guided percutaneous drainage, with open drainage as the fallback.
Why is a drainable abscess drained rather than opened at once?

choices.label: Drainage empties the pus with less surgery; antibiotics treat infection
Removing the appendix at the same time finishes the job
Only surgery cures, so a drain is never real treatment
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what the pus is, and which route removes it with the least operation. Which reason does that?
Yes. Image-guided drainage empties the pus without a laparotomy, and antibiotics treat the infection. Surgery is kept for failure.
Tempting: removing the appendix at once seems to settle the infection, leaving the pus with no source.
Not quite: a drainable abscess is first drained, with antibiotics. Surgery follows if drainage fails.
What is the first step for pus you can drain?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold the sequence: drain the pus first, then decide about the appendix.

say.text: Tempting: appendicitis is treated by removing the appendix, so that feels like the one real cure.
Not quite: appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, not the only one. A drainable collection is treated by drainage.
What can drain the collection without an operation?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: treatment of choice does not mean only treatment, and a collection is drained first.

say.text: Percutaneous drainage empties the pus under image guidance, and open drainage is the fallback if it fails. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, but not the only route.
Which of these is a complication of the operation, not of the disease?

choices.label: Pylephlebitis: portal vein infection with rigors and liver abscesses
Faecal fistula, from a slipped stump ligature or caecal necrosis
Appendicular mass, with omentum walling off the inflamed appendix
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether each item comes from the inflamed appendix before any knife, or from the wound and the stump after it.
Yes. A faecal fistula comes from the operation: a slipped stump ligature, or caecal necrosis.
Wound infection is the most common complication after appendicectomy.
Tempting: pylephlebitis is a severe infection that can follow appendix surgery, so it feels like an operative risk.
Not quite: it is septic thrombophlebitis of the portal veins, spread from the inflamed appendix, and it is a disease complication.
Does this complication come from the disease or from the knife?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace it: pylephlebitis belongs to the disease, and it can occur without any operation.

say.text: Tempting: a lump in the abdomen after an operation is common, so the mass seems like a surgical complication.
Not quite: the mass forms before surgery, when omentum and bowel wall off the inflamed appendix.
Is the mass a result of the disease or of the knife?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace it: the mass is part of the disease course, not the operation.

say.text: Disease complications come from the inflamed appendix: perforation, mass, abscess and pylephlebitis. Operation complications come from the knife: wound infection, faecal fistula and stump appendicitis.
Which is NOT a complication of acute appendicitis before any operation?

choices.label: Pylephlebitis, spreading through the portal veins
Stump appendicitis, from a long appendix stump
Appendicular abscess, with pus walled off
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which complication needs an operation to have happened first. Which option needs an operation?
Yes. Stump appendicitis comes from a long stump left at operation, so it is a complication of appendicectomy.
Pylephlebitis, abscess and perforation all arise from the disease itself.
Tempting: pylephlebitis is dangerous and can be found after surgery, so it looks like an operative complication.
Not quite: pylephlebitis is a disease complication, septic thrombophlebitis of the portal veins from the inflamed appendix.
Which list does it belong on, and what sits on the other list?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so sort the lists: disease first, then the knife.

say.text: Tempting: abscess is a word you link with post-operative infection, so it sounds like a surgical complication.
Not quite: an appendicular abscess is pus from the inflamed appendix, walled off before any surgery.
Which list does a pre-operative abscess sit on?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the origin: an abscess is a disease complication.

say.text: Stump appendicitis comes from the operation, when a long stump is left behind. Pylephlebitis and appendicular abscess come from the disease, before surgery.
A gridiron incision is made through McBurney's point. Which nerve injury can cause a right inguinal hernia?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The stem names the incision. Think about which nerve lies in the path of a cut through the muscle layers at that point.
Yes. The gridiron splits the oblique muscles along their fibres, and the ilioinguinal nerve is at risk.
Injury to that nerve causes a right inguinal hernia.
Tempting: it is a neighbour in the same list of iliac nerves, so it is the one you recall near the incision.
Not quite: the hernia that follows a gridiron injury is named for the ilioinguinal nerve, not its neighbour.
Which nerve does that hernia name?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair the incision with its nerve: gridiron and ilioinguinal.

say.text: Tempting: the genitofemoral nerve lies in the same iliac and groin region, so it seems to be the nerve at the incision.
Not quite: the gridiron is an oblique split of the muscles, and the nerve injured in it is the ilioinguinal.
Which of the three nerves is the one named for the hernia?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair the nerve with its complication: ilioinguinal injury gives a right inguinal hernia.

say.text: The gridiron splits the oblique muscles at McBurney's point. The ilioinguinal nerve is at risk, and its injury leads to a right inguinal hernia.
A 28-year-old has a right groin bulge and groin numbness after open appendicectomy through McBurney's point.
Which nerve was most likely injured?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Match the symptoms to the nerve that runs through the path of a gridiron cut. Which nerve causes a groin bulge after that cut?
Yes. A groin bulge and numbness after a gridiron cut point to the ilioinguinal nerve, with a right inguinal hernia.
Tempting: it is the other nerve you learned in the same iliac group, so the list pulls you towards it.
Not quite: the nerve that gives a groin hernia after a gridiron cut is the ilioinguinal.
Which nerve does the picture in the stem point to?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the picture: groin bulge and numbness after a gridiron cut means ilioinguinal.

say.text: Tempting: the femoral nerve is the big nerve of the groin, so the groin symptoms seem to point to it.
Not quite: the gridiron is in the iliac region, above the groin. The injured nerve is the ilioinguinal, and its injury causes the hernia.
Which nerve lies in the path of that incision?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so place the incision first, then the nerve.

say.text: Case by case: the bulge and numbness follow a gridiron cut, and the ilioinguinal nerve is the one injured. That injury leads to the right inguinal hernia.
Operate, wait or drain: uncomplicated disease can go to antibiotics-first in selected adults, a mass waits on the regimen, and a drainable abscess is drained.
Complications are sorted by origin: disease first, then the knife.
